angleRead.name: Rachel Torres
angleRead.text: Standing on the corner of 14th and Fruitvale, watching the evening crowd move between the taquerias and the bus stop, I keep coming back to the same number: nine incidents in San Antonio, one more than last cycle, and yet the clearance rate sits at 21 percent. That means roughly two out of every nine calls end with someone answering for it. The response time is 10.4 minutes — not the slowest in the city, but not fast enough when you're the one waiting. I want to walk the blocks where those nine calls came in, talk to the people on the porches, find out what they saw and what they think got missed. The property index at 36 and violent index at 27 tell me this isn't just one kind of trouble —

plan.focus: San Antonio's nine incidents and the gap between calls, charges, and custody
plan.why: San Antonio leads the city in incidents this cycle, yet its clearance rate and custody numbers suggest a disconnect between what gets reported and what gets resolved. That gap is where public trust either holds or breaks.
checks: Confirm the nine incidents in San Antonio and the one-incident increase from the prior cycle
Verify the 10.4-minute response time and 21% clearance rate for San Antonio
Cross-check the property index of 36 and violent index of 27 against the citywide picture
Confirm the custody trail: 9 charges, 2 arrests, 4 in custody at close for San Antonio
Compare San Antonio's numbers against the neighborhoods with the fewest incidents — Lake Merritt, Jack London, Downtown
plan.interpretation: The numbers suggest a neighborhood that is actively reporting trouble but not seeing it move through the system. The low clearance rate paired with the modest custody count points to either resource constraints or a classification gap — incidents logged but not pursued to arrest. The rise from last cycle adds urgency.
unverifiedLead: Residents on the Fruitvale side of San Antonio have mentioned calls that don't seem to go anywhere — reports filed, no follow-up, no one contacted afterward
A neighborhood watch volunteer said the same addresses keep coming up in the incident log, which might mean the response isn't addressing the root cause
There may be a pattern in what types of incidents get cleared versus which ones stall — property versus violent, daytime versus nighttime
plan.closeQuestion: Why does a neighborhood with the most incidents in the city see so few of them end in an arrest?
